content.title: About
content.content: Lemon juice, 100 % freshly squeezed, is obtained from ripe lemons without added sugar, preservatives or flavorings. It has a bright, refreshing taste and characteristic aroma, retaining most of the vitamins and minerals of the original fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lemons are among the oldest cultivated citrus fruits – they have been grown for over 2,500 years.
Freshly squeezed juice retains up to 90 % of vitamin C, which degrades quickly with heat.
Lemon juice is often used as a natural preservative in cooking because of its acidity (pH ≈ 2.5).
The juice helps improve iron absorption from plant foods.
In traditional medicine, lemon juice is used to support digestion and detoxification.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Acids in the juice stimulate gastric juice production, enhancing food breakdown.

items.title: Improves iron absorption
items.content: Ascorbic acid increases the bioavailability of non‑heme iron from plant sources.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Besides vitamin C, the juice contains flavonoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The juice is almost entirely water, helping maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Tooth enamel erosion
items.content: Frequent consumption of acidic drinks may contribute to enamel erosion; rinsing the mouth with water afterward is recommended.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to citrus fruits.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: The acids in lemon juice can affect the absorption of certain drugs, such as some antibiotics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lemon juice can be added to water, tea, sauces, marinades, baked goods and desserts. It is commonly used as a salad dressing or to make lemonade. If desired, dilute the juice with water in a 1:4 ratio for a milder flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator in a tightly sealed bottle for no more than 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze it in portioned ice cubes. Discard the juice if its color changes, it develops an off‑smell, or sediment appears.
